title: Μενελάου δῶμα
about: Telemachus and Peisistratus, Nestor's son, arrive at Sparta in the middle of a double wedding feast in the halls of Menelaus, who is marrying off his son Megapenthes and sending his daughter Hermione to the son of Achilles. The steward Eteoneus spots the two strangers and asks whether to receive them; Menelaus rebukes him for hesitating and orders the horses stabled and the guests welcomed, bathed, fed, and seated at his own table. Telemachus, awed by the gold, amber, silver, and ivory that fill the palace, quietly marvels to his companion that even the halls of Olympian Zeus can hardly surpass it. Overhearing him, Menelaus admits that his wealth came at a bitter cost: eight years of wandering, the murder of his brother, and, above all, an unhealed grief for Odysseus, whose fate is still unknown to his own father, wife, and son.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἷξον κοίλην Λακεδαίμονα κητώεσσαν,
πρὸς δ’ ἄρα δώματ’ ἔλων Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο.
sentences.l:
And they came to hollow Lacedaemon, full-of-ravines,
and to the halls then they drove of Menelaus, glorious.
sentences.i: They came to hollow Lacedaemon, land of many ravines, and drove on to the halls of glorious Menelaus.
sentences.n: ἷξον is the unaugmented aorist of ἵκω/ἱκνέομαι, 'arrive at' (Attic ἷκον); the subject is Telemachus and Peisistratus, continuing from Book 3. κητώεσσα, the epithet fixed to Lacedaemon, is of disputed formation: the usual gloss is 'full of hollows, ravines' (from a noun κῆτος 'cavity'), though the ancients sometimes connected it with the other κῆτος 'sea-monster'; the meaning is not certain. ἔλων is the unaugmented aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive', used of chariots. κυδαλίμοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου) of κυδάλιμος 'glorious', from κῦδος 'glory'; paired with Μενελάου it recurs at 4.16, 4.23 and 4.46, and is rendered the same way each time.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ εὗρον δαινύντα γάμον πολλοῖσιν ἔτῃσιν
υἱέος ἠδὲ θυγατρὸς ἀμύμονος ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
sentences.l:
And him they found feasting a wedding for his many kinsmen,
of his son and of his blameless daughter, in his own house.
sentences.i: They found him in his own house, holding a wedding feast for many of his kinsmen, for his son and his blameless daughter.
sentences.n: εὗρον is the unaugmented aorist of εὑρίσκω. δαινύντα is the present participle of δαίνυμι 'give a feast', governing γάμον as its object, 'feasting a wedding', i.e. holding a wedding banquet. ἔτῃσιν is dative plural of ἔτης 'kinsman, clansman' (not to be confused with ἔτος 'year'). ἀμύμονος is the fixed epithet 'blameless' (see the house table), here given to Menelaus's own daughter Hermione, named only at 4.14. ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ shows the possessive ὅς again, with ἐνί an adverb, 'in his own house'.

sentences.t: τὴν μὲν Ἀχιλλῆος ῥηξήνορος υἱέι πέμπεν·
sentences.l: The girl he was sending to the son of Achilles, breaker-of-ranks;
sentences.i: He was sending his daughter to the son of Achilles, breaker of the ranks of men;
sentences.n: τήν is the pronoun, 'her', referring forward to Hermione. πέμπεν is an unaugmented imperfect, 'was sending'. ῥηξήνωρ, 'breaking the ranks of men' (ῥήγνυμι + ἀνήρ), is a standing epithet of Achilles alone in Homer; his son is Neoptolemus, though the name is not given here. The line closes with an ano teleia, since the two grounds for the marriage follow at once.

sentences.t:
ἐν Τροίῃ γὰρ πρῶτον ὑπέσχετο καὶ κατένευσε
δωσέμεναι, τοῖσιν δὲ θεοὶ γάμον ἐξετέλειον.
sentences.l:
for at Troy first he had promised and had nodded assent
to give her, and for them the gods were bringing the marriage to fulfillment.
sentences.i: for at Troy he had first promised, and pledged with a nod, to give her to him, and now the gods were bringing that marriage to pass.
sentences.n: ὑπέσχετο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ὑπισχνέομαι 'promise'. κατένευσε, from κατανεύω 'nod down, assent', is the gesture by which a promise is sealed, most famously Zeus's nod at Iliad 1.528. δωσέμεναι is a future infinitive in -έμεναι, 'that he would give'. τοῖσιν is the pronoun dative, 'for them', the young couple. ἐξετέλειον is an unaugmented imperfect of ἐκτελέω 'bring fully to completion', apt for a promise now being carried out.

sentences.t:
τὴν ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ἔνθ’ ἵπποισι καὶ ἅρμασι πέμπε νέεσθαι
Μυρμιδόνων προτὶ ἄστυ περικλυτόν, οἷσιν ἄνασσεν.
sentences.l:
Her, then, he, thither, with horses and with chariot was sending to go
to the Myrmidons' city far-renowned, over whom he was lord.
sentences.i: So he was sending her off with horses and chariot to travel there, to the far-famed city of the Myrmidons, over whom Achilles' son ruled.
sentences.n: ἄρα (elided ἄρ’) marks the natural sequel to what was just said. ὅ γε is the pronoun, 'he', Menelaus. νέεσθαι is uncontracted (Attic νεῖσθαι), 'to go, journey', an infinitive of purpose after πέμπε. περικλυτόν, 'famed all round', is a general epithet of a city, from περί and κλυτός 'renowned'; the city itself is not named. οἷσιν is the possessive ὅς, 'over whom, his own'; the unaugmented imperfect ἄνασσεν, 'was lord of', has as its subject Achilles' son, the bridegroom of the previous unit, though the shift from Menelaus is left unmarked.

sentences.t:
υἱέι δὲ Σπάρτηθεν Ἀλέκτορος ἤγετο κούρην,
ὅς οἱ τηλύγετος γένετο κρατερὸς Μεγαπένθης
ἐκ δούλης·
sentences.i: For his son — Megapenthes the mighty, the late-born child a slave-woman had borne him — he was fetching home from Sparta the daughter of Alector;
sentences.n: ἤγετο is an unaugmented imperfect middle of ἄγω, used of leading home a bride. Σπάρτηθεν has the suffix -θεν, 'from', attached to the place-name; Sparta and Lacedaemon (4.1) are Homer's two names for the same region, kept as distinct English words since Murray's Greek keeps them distinct. τηλύγετος is a standing epithet of a child whose meaning is not securely known: the usual gloss is 'late-born', though 'tenderly loved, darling' has also been argued, and neither etymology is certain. κρατερός is the ordinary epithet 'mighty, strong'. ἐκ δούλης, 'from a slave-woman', names Megapenthes as Menelaus's son by a concubine, not by Helen; the relative clause ὅς...ἐκ δούλης, though placed after the main verb, in fact identifies which son (υἱέι, 4.10) receives the bride.

sentences.t:
Ἑλένῃ δὲ θεοὶ γόνον οὐκέτ’ ἔφαινον,
ἐπεὶ δὴ τὸ πρῶτον ἐγείνατο παῖδ’ ἐρατεινήν,
Ἑρμιόνην, ἣ εἶδος ἔχε χρυσέης Ἀφροδίτης.
sentences.l:
But to Helen the gods no more were bringing-to-light offspring,
since indeed at the first she had borne a lovely child,
Hermione, who had the beauty of golden Aphrodite.
sentences.i: But the gods no longer granted Helen any child, once she had borne, at the very first, a lovely daughter, Hermione, who had the beauty of golden Aphrodite.
sentences.n: ἔφαινον, an unaugmented imperfect of φαίνω, here 'bring to light, grant the birth of'. ἐγείνατο is the unaugmented aorist middle of γείνομαι 'bear, beget'. τὸ πρῶτον is adverbial, 'at first, the first time'. This line carries the reviewer's flagged metrical irregularity at ἐπεί, where the transmitted text seems to need the first syllable long though ἐπεί is ordinarily short there; if that lengthening proves real rather than a licence of recitation, it marks a genuine roughness in the verse at this point. εἶδος ἔχε, 'had the look, form of', with the imperfect ἔχω, is a common way to compare a mortal's beauty to a god's; χρυσέης Ἀφροδίτης, 'golden Aphrodite', is her standing epithet.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν δαίνυντο καθ’ ὑψερεφὲς μέγα δῶμα
γείτονες ἠδὲ ἔται Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο,
τερπόμενοι·
sentences.i: So they feasted throughout the high-roofed great hall, the neighbors and kinsmen of glorious Menelaus, taking their pleasure;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν is the pronoun, 'they', the wedding guests. δαίνυντο is an unaugmented imperfect middle, 'were feasting', echoing δαινύντα of line 3. ὑψερεφής, 'high-roofed', joins ὑψι- 'high' and ἐρέφω 'roof over'; it recurs at 4.46 of the same house, and both instances are given the same English. γείτονες ἠδὲ ἔται pairs 'neighbors' with 'clansmen', the guests proper to a great household's wedding. τερπόμενοι, 'delighting themselves', looks forward to the entertainment that follows.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δέ σφιν ἐμέλπετο θεῖος ἀοιδὸς
φορμίζων, δοιὼ δὲ κυβιστητῆρε κατ’ αὐτούς,
μολπῆς ἐξάρχοντος, ἐδίνευον κατὰ μέσσους.
sentences.l:
and among them was making music the divine minstrel,
playing the lyre, and two tumblers among them,
while he led off the song, were whirling through their midst.
sentences.i: and among them the divine minstrel was making music, playing on the lyre, while two tumblers whirled about in their midst as he led the song.
sentences.n: ἐμέλπετο is an unaugmented imperfect middle of μέλπω 'sing and dance to music'. θεῖος ἀοιδός is the fixed formula already given to Phemius, 'the divine minstrel'; this minstrel is unnamed. φορμίζων is from φόρμιγξ, the lyre. δοιώ and κυβιστητῆρε are dual forms, 'two tumblers'; κυβιστάω is 'turn somersaults'. μολπῆς ἐξάρχοντος is a genitive absolute, 'while he led off the singing'. ἐδίνευον is an unaugmented imperfect of δινεύω, 'were whirling', of the acrobats' spinning dance among the guests.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ αὖτ’ ἐν προθύροισι δόμων αὐτώ τε καὶ ἵππω,
Τηλέμαχός θ’ ἥρως καὶ Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱός,
στῆσαν·
sentences.i: But the two of them, Telemachus the hero and Nestor's splendid son, drew up in the forecourt of the house, themselves and their pair of horses;
sentences.n: τὼ δ’ αὖτ(ε) turns the scene from the feast back to the new arrivals; τώ, αὐτώ and ἵππω are all dual forms, as is the transitive aorist στῆσαν, 'they brought to a stand'. προθύροισι is the fixed 'forecourt' (see 3.493 in the house table). ἥρως, 'the hero', is the fixed title used of Telemachus (see the house table). Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱός names Peisistratus by patronymic and epithet only; he is never named outright anywhere in this part, and ἀγλαός keeps the house-fixed 'splendid'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ προμολὼν ἴδετο κρείων Ἐτεωνεύς,
ὀτρηρὸς θεράπων Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἀγγελέων διὰ δώματα ποιμένι λαῶν,
ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And he, coming forward, caught sight of them, the lord Eteoneus,
the brisk attendant of Menelaus, glorious,
and he set out to go, to bring word, through the halls, to the shepherd of the people,
and standing close by, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: And the lord Eteoneus, coming out, caught sight of them — the brisk attendant of glorious Menelaus — and he set out through the halls to bring word to the shepherd of the people, and, standing close beside him, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: προμολών is the aorist participle of προβλώσκω 'come forth'. ἴδετο is unaugmented, middle in form though passive in sense, 'caught sight of'. κρείων, 'ruling, lordly', here honors the chief steward of the household rather than a king; it is kept as 'lord' to mark his standing among the servants. ὀτρηρὸς θεράπων, 'brisk attendant', recurs at 4.38 of the other servants and is rendered the same way both times. βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is the fixed formula for setting out, here with the future participle ἀγγελέων, 'to bring word'. ποιμένι λαῶν is the fixed 'shepherd of the people', here Menelaus. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the fixed formula 'winged words he spoke', closing the line before Eteoneus's own words begin.

sentences.t:
ξείνω δή τινε τώδε, διοτρεφὲς ὦ Μενέλαε,
ἄνδρε δύω, γενεῇ δὲ Διὸς μεγάλοιο ἔικτον.
sentences.l:
“Strangers, indeed, some two, these here, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus,
two men, and in lineage to great Zeus they seem alike.
sentences.i: “Here are two strangers, Zeus-nurtured Menelaus, two men who look, by their lineage, like the kin of great Zeus.
sentences.n: ξείνω, ἄνδρε, δύω, τώδε and ἔικτον are all dual forms, since two men have arrived together. διοτρεφής, 'Zeus-nurtured', is the house-fixed epithet already given to kings collectively (4.63) and applied here to Menelaus alone. ἔικτον is the dual perfect of ἔοικα, 'they seem, resemble', with γενεῇ a dative of respect, 'in birth, lineage'; Eteoneus judges the strangers noble by their bearing before he knows who they are.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴπ’, ἤ σφωιν καταλύσομεν ὠκέας ἵππους,
ἦ ἄλλον πέμπωμεν ἱκανέμεν, ὅς κε φιλήσῃ.
sentences.l:
But say, whether for them we should unyoke the swift horses,
or send them on to someone else, to arrive, who will entertain them.”
sentences.i: But tell me, are we to unyoke their swift horses, or send them on to someone else who will give them welcome?”
sentences.n: εἴπ’ is the aorist imperative εἰπέ, elided. σφωιν is the dual pronoun, 'for the two of them'. καταλύσομεν is a deliberative subjunctive with a short vowel (formally identical to a future), 'shall we unyoke'; ὠκέας ἵππους is the fixed 'swift horses' (see the house table). ἱκανέμεν, an infinitive in -έμεν, expresses purpose, 'to go on and arrive'. φιλήσῃ, subjunctive of φιλέω, here means 'give hospitality to, entertain', its ordinary sense with a guest as object.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: Him then, greatly vexed, addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: Then, greatly troubled, fair-haired Menelaus said to him:
sentences.n: ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω 'be vexed, be troubled', a verb regularly used before a rebuke or an outburst of feeling in Homer; μέγα as its adverb intensifies it, 'greatly'. προσέφη is the imperfect of πρόσφημι 'address'. ξανθὸς Μενέλαος, 'fair-haired Menelaus', is the fixed epithet-name pair (see the house table), used here for the first time in this part. Eteoneus's question about turning strangers away has visibly annoyed his master.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν νήπιος ἦσθα, Βοηθοΐδη Ἐτεωνεῦ,
τὸ πρίν·
sentences.l:
“Surely not foolish were you before this, Eteoneus, son of Boethous,
before now;
sentences.i: “You were not a fool before now, Eteoneus, son of Boethous;
sentences.n: νήπιος, 'without sense, foolish, childish', is a common word of mild or severe reproach in Homer. ἦσθα is the second singular imperfect of εἰμί, 'you were'. Βοηθοΐδη is the vocative patronymic, 'son of Boethous', otherwise unknown to the poem. τὸ πρίν, 'before this, formerly', is adverbial, and its ano teleia marks a real pause before the sharper contrast that follows.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ μὲν νῦν γε πάϊς ὣς νήπια βάζεις.
sentences.l: but now, at least, like a child, foolish things you babble.”
sentences.i: but now you are babbling like a child.”
sentences.n: ἀτάρ, 'but, however', introduces the sharp turn from the concession just made. πάϊς ὥς, with ὥς accented and postpositive, means 'like a child' (Attic ὡς παῖς); νήπια is a neuter plural used adverbially with βάζεις, 'you talk foolish things', echoing νήπιος from the line before. βάζω is properly 'chatter, babble', with a note of contempt here.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν δὴ νῶι ξεινήια πολλὰ φαγόντε
ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων δεῦρ’ ἱκόμεθ’, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς
ἐξοπίσω περ παύσῃ ὀιζύος.
sentences.l:
Surely indeed we two, having eaten much hospitality
of other men, have come here, in the hope that somewhere Zeus
hereafter, at least, may make us cease from misery.
sentences.i: Why, the two of us have come here after eating the hospitality of many other men, hoping that Zeus may someday, later on, put an end to our misery.
sentences.n: νῶι is the dual pronoun 'we two', Menelaus and his household on their own long travels home from Troy; φαγόντε is the dual aorist participle of ἐσθίω. ξεινήια, 'guest-gifts, hospitality', is a noun built on ξένος. ἱκόμεθ’ is the unaugmented aorist middle, 'we have come'. αἴ κε with the subjunctive παύσῃ expresses a hope, 'in case Zeus may...'. ἐξοπίσω, 'hereafter, in time to come', with περ, gives the hope a note of patience: not yet, but someday.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ λύ’ ἵππους
ξείνων, ἐς δ’ αὐτοὺς προτέρω ἄγε θοινηθῆναι.
sentences.l:
But loose the horses
of the strangers, and them further in bring, to be feasted.”
sentences.i: So unyoke the strangers' horses, and bring the men themselves further in, to be feasted.”
sentences.n: λύ’ is the present imperative λύε, elided. ξείνων is a possessive genitive, 'of the strangers'. ἐς...προτέρω ἄγε is a directional phrase with the imperative ἄγε, 'lead further in'; θοινηθῆναι is a passive infinitive of purpose, 'to be feasted'. Menelaus's answer directly reverses the question Eteoneus asked, ordering full hospitality without hesitation.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δὲ μεγάροιο διέσσυτο, κέκλετο δ’ ἄλλους
ὀτρηροὺς θεράποντας ἅμα σπέσθαι ἑοῖ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he sped out through the hall, and called to other
brisk attendants together to follow along with him.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Eteoneus hurried out through the hall, and called on the other brisk attendants to follow along with him.
sentences.n: φάθ’ is φάτο, the imperfect of φημί; the formula 'so he spoke' is fixed (see the house table), though here it opens a new clause rather than standing alone. διέσσυτο is an unaugmented aorist (imperfect in form) of διασεύομαι, 'rush through'. κέκλετο is the unaugmented aorist of κέλομαι, 'call on, bid'. ὀτρηροὺς θεράποντας, 'brisk attendants', repeats the phrase used of Eteoneus himself at 4.23, now of his fellow servants. σπέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of ἕπομαι 'follow'; ἑοῖ αὐτῷ is 'with him himself', an emphatic dative.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἵππους μὲν λῦσαν ὑπὸ ζυγοῦ ἱδρώοντας,
καὶ τοὺς μὲν κατέδησαν ἐφ’ ἱππείῃσι κάπῃσι,
πὰρ δ’ ἔβαλον ζειάς, ἀνὰ δὲ κρῖ λευκὸν ἔμιξαν,
ἅρματα δ’ ἔκλιναν πρὸς ἐνώπια παμφανόωντα,
sentences.l:
And they loosed the horses, sweating, from under the yoke,
and these they tethered at the horses' mangers,
and beside them threw spelt, and in it white barley they mixed,
and the chariot leaned against the shining inner wall,
sentences.i: The men loosed the sweating horses from under the yoke, tethered them at the horse-stalls, threw down spelt for them and mixed in white barley, and leaned the chariot against the gleaming inner wall of the porch,
sentences.n: This four-line stretch is cut at a comma rather than run on to the next full stop, since the sentence does not close until partway through line 43, more than four lines from its start. ἱππείῃσι κάπῃσι is a dative plural, 'at the horse-mangers'. ζειαί is spelt or emmer, a coarse grain fed to horses beside barley (κρῖ, an indeclinable form of κριθή). παμφανόωντα is a present participle with diectasis (from παμφαίνω), 'all-shining'; ἐνώπια are the inner wall-faces of the porch, opposite the entrance, a fixed piece of household architecture in epic.

sentences.t: αὐτοὺς δ’ εἰσῆγον θεῖον δόμον.
sentences.l: and the men themselves they led into the divine house.
sentences.i: and led the men themselves into the divine house.
sentences.n: εἰσῆγον is an unaugmented imperfect of εἰσάγω. θεῖον δόμον, 'the divine house', uses the fixed adjective θεῖος, 'divine' (see the house table entry for the divine minstrel); applied here to a mortal's hall it marks its splendor as more than ordinary, not that the house is literally sacred.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ ἰδόντες
θαύμαζον κατὰ δῶμα διοτρεφέος βασιλῆος·
sentences.l:
And they, having seen it,
were marveling throughout the house of the Zeus-nurtured king;
sentences.i: And at the sight of it they marveled throughout the house of the Zeus-nurtured king;
sentences.n: ἰδόντες is the unaugmented aorist participle of ὁράω. θαύμαζον is an unaugmented imperfect, 'were marveling'. διοτρεφέος βασιλῆος, 'of the Zeus-nurtured king', echoes the plural διοτρεφέων βασιλήων already fixed at 4.63, here in the singular, of Menelaus himself; the adjective is translated the same way in both numbers.

sentences.t:
ὥς τε γὰρ ἠελίου αἴγλη πέλεν ἠὲ σελήνης
δῶμα καθ’ ὑψερεφὲς Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο.
sentences.l:
for it was as though the radiance of the sun, or the moon's,
filled the high-roofed house of Menelaus, glorious.
sentences.i: for it was as if the radiance of the sun or the moon filled the high-roofed house of glorious Menelaus.
sentences.n: ὥς τε with the indicative πέλεν introduces a simile of general truth, 'it was just as if'; πέλεν is the unaugmented imperfect of πέλω 'be'. αἴγλη is 'brightness, radiance'. ὑψερεφές and Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο both repeat, word for word, phrases already fixed earlier in this part (4.15–16, 4.46), and are rendered exactly as before.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τάρπησαν ὁρώμενοι ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
ἔς ῥ’ ἀσαμίνθους βάντες ἐυξέστας λούσαντο.
sentences.l:
But when they had had their fill, looking with their eyes,
into well-smoothed bathing-tubs they stepped, and washed.
sentences.i: But when they had feasted their eyes to the full, they stepped into well-polished bathing-tubs and washed.
sentences.n: τάρπησαν is the aorist passive, intransitive in sense, of τέρπω, 'take one's fill of delight'; ὁρώμενοι ὀφθαλμοῖσιν, 'looking with the eyes', is added for emphasis, since τέρπομαι alone would already imply pleasure. ἀσαμίνθους is the accusative plural of ἀσάμινθος, a bathtub, a word whose ultimate origin is unknown, though the bath scene it belongs to recurs elsewhere in the poem (cf. 3.467–468 in the house table). ἐυξέστας, 'well-planed, well-polished', describes the tub's smoothed wood or stone.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν δμῳαὶ λοῦσαν καὶ χρῖσαν ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρα χλαίνας οὔλας βάλον ἠδὲ χιτῶνας,
ἔς ῥα θρόνους ἕζοντο παρ’ Ἀτρεΐδην Μενέλαον.
sentences.l:
And them, when then the slave-women had bathed and anointed with oil,
and about them had thrown thick cloaks and tunics,
they sat down on chairs, beside Atreus' son Menelaus.
sentences.i: And when the serving-women had bathed and anointed them with oil, and put thick cloaks and tunics about them, they sat down on chairs beside Menelaus, son of Atreus.
sentences.n: λοῦσαν and χρῖσαν are unaugmented aorists, third plural, of λούω and χρίω. οὔλας, 'thick, woolly', describes the cloaks' nap. ἕζοντο is an unaugmented imperfect middle, 'were seating themselves'. Ἀτρεΐδην Μενέλαον follows the pattern already fixed for Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι in the house table, 'Atreus' son', here for Menelaus rather than his brother; θρόνος, unlike the plainer δίφρος, is a chair of some dignity, fit for honored guests.

sentences.t:
χέρνιβα δ’ ἀμφίπολος προχόῳ ἐπέχευε φέρουσα
καλῇ χρυσείῃ ὑπὲρ ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος,
νίψασθαι·
sentences.i: A handmaid brought water for the hands in a fine golden pitcher and poured it over a silver basin, for them to wash;
sentences.n: This whole span is identical, word for word, to a line already shipped at 2.136 (odyssey-002, of the suitors' meal); the same formula of hospitality serves both houses, and the English here matches what was ratified there exactly, as the convention requires for a repeated whole unit. χέρνιβα is 'water for washing the hands'; προχόῳ is the pitcher it is poured from; νίψασθαι is a middle infinitive of purpose, 'for washing themselves'.

sentences.t: παρὰ δὲ ξεστὴν ἐτάνυσσε τράπεζαν.
sentences.l: and beside them she stretched out a polished table.
sentences.i: and she drew up a polished table beside them.
sentences.n: ἐτάνυσσε is the aorist of τανύω 'stretch, draw out', here of setting up a table for the meal. ξεστήν, 'scraped smooth, polished', describes the finish of good household furniture; the same handmaid of the previous unit continues the action.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δ’ αἰδοίη ταμίη παρέθηκε φέρουσα,
εἴδατα πόλλ’ ἐπιθεῖσα, χαριζομένη παρεόντων.
sentences.l:
And bread a revered housekeeper set beside them, bringing it,
and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what was at hand.
sentences.i: A revered housekeeper brought bread and set it beside them, and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what she had by her.
sentences.n: This same two-line sentence has already been shipped, word for word, at 2.139–140, where it ends with an ano teleia because the sentence continues further in that part; Murray's text for Book 4 closes it instead with a full stop, so the English wording is kept and only the terminal mark follows this edition. αἰδοίη ταμίη, 'a revered housekeeper', is the house-fixed epithet-noun pair; χαριζομένη, 'graciously giving', takes the partitive genitive παρεόντων, 'of what was to hand'.

sentences.t:
δαιτρὸς δὲ κρειῶν πίνακας παρέθηκεν ἀείρας
παντοίων, παρὰ δέ σφι τίθει χρύσεια κύπελλα.
sentences.l:
and a carver lifted and set beside them platters of meats
of all kinds, and beside them was setting golden cups.
sentences.i: and a carver lifted platters of meats of every kind and set them by, and was putting golden cups at their side.
sentences.n: As at 4.55–56, this two-line sentence repeats one already shipped at 2.141, again ending here with a full stop where the earlier occurrence had an ano teleia because its own sentence ran on; the wording is unchanged, only the terminal mark follows this edition. δαιτρός is 'a carver, one who portions out meat'; ἀείρας is the aorist participle of ἀείρω, 'having lifted up'. τίθει is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι, 'was setting out'.

sentences.t: τὼ καὶ δεικνύμενος προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: And to the two of them, gesturing, spoke fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: And gesturing toward the food, fair-haired Menelaus said to the two of them:
sentences.n: τώ is again the dual pronoun, 'to the two of them', Telemachus and Peisistratus. δεικνύμενος is the present middle participle of δείκνυμι, 'pointing out, showing'; here it marks Menelaus gesturing at the meal as he invites them to it, a variant of the introductory formulas already fixed for his speeches, though this particular participle occurs only this once in the part.

sentences.t: σίτου θ’ ἅπτεσθον καὶ χαίρετον.
sentences.l: “Of food, the two of you, take hold, and rejoice.
sentences.i: “Take hold of the food, the two of you, and welcome.
sentences.n: ἅπτεσθον and χαίρετον are dual imperatives, addressed to Telemachus and Peisistratus together. σίτου is a genitive with ἅπτομαι, 'lay hold of, partake of'. χαῖρε, ξεῖνε, 'Welcome, stranger', is fixed elsewhere in the house table as a greeting; here the dual χαίρετον serves the same welcoming function toward two guests at once.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
δείπνου πασσαμένω εἰρησόμεθ’, οἵ τινές ἐστον
ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.i: and afterward, once the two of you have had your fill of the meal, we will ask who you are, and of what men;
sentences.n: πασσαμένω is a dual aorist participle of πατέομαι 'taste, partake of', governing the genitive δείπνου. εἰρησόμεθ’ is a future middle, 'we shall ask'; ἐστόν is the dual second person of εἰμί. The postponed question, 'who you are, of what men', is a standard courtesy in Homer: hospitality precedes inquiry, and a guest eats before he is asked his name.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ σφῷν γε γένος ἀπόλωλε τοκήων,
ἀλλ’ ἀνδρῶν γένος ἐστὲ διοτρεφέων βασιλήων
σκηπτούχων, ἐπεὶ οὔ κε κακοὶ τοιούσδε τέκοιεν.
sentences.i: for the line of your parents is surely not lost in you two; you are of the stock of Zeus-nurtured, scepter-bearing kings, since common men could not have fathered sons like you.”
sentences.n: σφῷν is the dual genitive pronoun, 'of you two'. γένος τοκήων is 'the stock, line of parents'; ἀπόλωλε is a perfect of ἀπόλλυμι, 'has been lost, died out'. διοτρεφέων βασιλήων, 'of Zeus-nurtured kings', repeats exactly the house-fixed formula (see the table); σκηπτοῦχος, 'holding the scepter', is a further mark of royal rank. τέκοιεν is an optative in a clause of unreal or general condition, 'men could not have begotten'.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, καί σφιν νῶτα βοὸς παρὰ πίονα θῆκεν
ὄπτ’ ἐν χερσὶν ἑλών, τά ῥά οἱ γέρα πάρθεσαν αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and beside them the fat chine of an ox he set down,
roasted, in his hands having taken it, which as his own prize had been set before him.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and taking up in his own hands the fat roasted chine of beef that had been set before him as his prize of honor, he set it down beside them.
sentences.n: The fixed formula 'so he spoke' opens the sentence, though here it runs directly into the next clause rather than standing alone (contrast 4.37, where it likewise continues, and 1.42–43 in the pilot part, where it stands with an ano teleia by itself). νῶτα...πίονα is 'the fat chine, back-piece'; ὄπτα is a predicate adjective, 'roasted'. γέρας is a portion of honor set aside for a person of rank at a feast; πάρθεσαν is an unaugmented aorist of παρατίθημι, 'had set before'. Menelaus gives the newcomers his own choice cut, a mark of high honor.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: This line is identical, word for word, to one already shipped at 2.149, of the suitors' meal, and the English here matches it exactly. ὀνείατα is 'good things (to eat)'; ἴαλλον is an unaugmented imperfect of ἰάλλω 'send forth, put out'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
δὴ τότε Τηλέμαχος προσεφώνεε Νέστορος υἱόν,
ἄγχι σχὼν κεφαλήν, ἵνα μὴ πευθοίαθ’ οἱ ἄλλοι·
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
then at last Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor,
holding his head close, so that the others should not hear:
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, then Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor, holding his head close, so that the others should not hear:
sentences.n: The first line is the house-fixed formula already shipped at 1.150, 3.67, 3.473 and 2.150, and is translated exactly as ratified there. The third line, 'holding his head close...so that the others should not hear', is likewise already shipped, at 2.157, of Telemachus speaking privately to the disguised Athena; the same wording is kept here, but without the earlier 'to hers', since the listener is now a man, Nestor's son, not a goddess. προσεφώνεε is an unaugmented imperfect of προσφωνέω, 'spoke to, addressed'.

sentences.t:
φράζεο, Νεστορίδη, τῷ ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ,
χαλκοῦ τε στεροπὴν κὰδ δώματα ἠχήεντα
χρυσοῦ τ’ ἠλέκτρου τε καὶ ἀργύρου ἠδ’ ἐλέφαντος.
sentences.l:
“Mark, son of Nestor, dear to my own heart,
the flash of bronze throughout the echoing halls,
and of gold and of amber and of silver and of ivory.
sentences.i: “Mark this, son of Nestor, you who are dear to my heart — the gleam of bronze through these echoing halls, and of gold and amber and silver and ivory.
sentences.n: φράζεο is a present middle imperative, 'take note, observe'. Νεστορίδη is the vocative patronymic, 'son of Nestor'. κεχαρισμένε is the perfect passive participle of χαρίζομαι, vocative, 'made pleasing, dear'. κὰδ δώματα shows tmesis with apocope: κατά shortened to κάδ before δ-, the phrase meaning 'throughout the halls'. ἠχήεντα, 'echoing, resounding', marks the hall's size. The four genitives, bronze, gold, amber, silver, ivory, list the materials whose gleam so strikes Telemachus.

sentences.t:
Ζηνός που τοιήδε γ’ Ὀλυμπίου ἔνδοθεν αὐλή,
ὅσσα τάδ’ ἄσπετα πολλά·
sentences.l:
Of Zeus, I suppose, such as this, at least, within is the court,
Olympian's, so much unspeakable wealth is here;
sentences.i: The court within the house of Olympian Zeus himself must surely be like this, such untold abundance is here;
sentences.n: που is 'I suppose, perhaps', an epistemic particle softening the claim. τοιήδε...αὐλή, 'a court such as this', with γε emphasizing 'at least this much'. ἔνδοθεν, 'from within, within', is adverbial. ἄσπετα, 'unspeakable, unutterable', from ἀ- and the root of ἔπος, intensifies πολλά; Telemachus, prince of a far poorer household on Ithaca, compares Menelaus's wealth to the palace of a god.

sentences.t: σέβας μ’ ἔχει εἰσορόωντα.
sentences.l: Awe holds me as I gaze upon it.”
sentences.i: Wonder comes over me as I look at it.”
sentences.n: σέβας is 'awe, reverent wonder'; ἔχει, 'holds, possesses (me)', is the ordinary Homeric idiom for a feeling that overtakes someone. εἰσορόωντα is a present participle with diectasis (from εἰσοράω), accusative agreeing with the unexpressed 'me', 'as I look on it'.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀγορεύοντος ξύνετο ξανθὸς Μενέλαος,
καί σφεας φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And while he was speaking, understood him fair-haired Menelaus,
and having spoken to them, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Fair-haired Menelaus caught what he was saying, and speaking up to them, spoke winged words:
sentences.n: τοῦ...ἀγορεύοντος is a genitive absolute, 'while he was speaking'; ξύνετο is an unaugmented aorist of συνίημι, 'understood, took in', with the genitive of the person heard. σφεας is 'them', the two young men. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the fixed formula, repeated here a third time in this part (see 4.25, 4.77).

sentences.t: τέκνα φίλ’, ἦ τοι Ζηνὶ βροτῶν οὐκ ἄν τις ἐρίζοι·
sentences.l: “Dear children, truly, indeed, with Zeus no mortal could ever vie;
sentences.i: “Dear children, no mortal could ever rival Zeus;
sentences.n: τέκνα φίλα, 'dear children', addresses both young men together, in place of individual vocatives. ἦ τοι, an emphatic combination, opens the general truth that follows. ἐρίζοι is a potential optative with ἄν, 'could vie, contend'; the dative Ζηνί is the person contended with, the regular Homeric construction of ἐρίζω.

sentences.t: ἀθάνατοι γὰρ τοῦ γε δόμοι καὶ κτήματ’ ἔασιν·
sentences.l: for immortal are his house and his possessions, at least;
sentences.i: for his house and his possessions are immortal;
sentences.n: τοῦ γε is the pronoun, 'his, at least', i.e. Zeus's. ἔασιν is the epic third plural of εἰμί (Attic εἰσίν). The line explains why no rivalry with Zeus is possible: a god's wealth does not perish as a mortal's can, the very point Menelaus goes on to qualify about his own house.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρῶν δ’ ἤ κέν τίς μοι ἐρίσσεται, ἠὲ καὶ οὐκί,
κτήμασιν.
sentences.l:
But of men, either someone might rival me, or else not,
in possessions.
sentences.i: But among men, someone might perhaps rival me in possessions, or perhaps not.
sentences.n: ἐρίσσεται is a short-vowel aorist subjunctive (= ἐρίσσηται) used with κέν in a general future sense, 'might vie with me'; the dative μοι is 'with me'. ἠὲ καὶ οὐκί, 'or else not', leaves the claim deliberately open, a modesty formula before Menelaus qualifies his wealth with the grief that came with it.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ πολλὰ παθὼν καὶ πόλλ’ ἐπαληθεὶς
ἠγαγόμην ἐν νηυσὶ καὶ ὀγδοάτῳ ἔτει ἦλθον,
Κύπρον Φοινίκην τε καὶ Αἰγυπτίους ἐπαληθείς,
sentences.i: For indeed, after much suffering and much wandering, I brought my wealth home in my ships and came back in the eighth year, having wandered to Cyprus and Phoenicia and the land of the Egyptians,
sentences.n: This clause runs past four lines before its first full stop, at the end of line 85, so it is cut here instead at the comma where the sense pauses most naturally, before Menelaus lists his further destinations. παθών and the repeated ἐπαληθείς are both aorist participles, beside the finite unaugmented aorists ἠγαγόμην and ἦλθον. ἠγαγόμην, 'I brought home for myself', is middle, marking personal gain. The eight years mark how long Menelaus's own return from Troy took, far longer than a direct voyage.

sentences.t:
Αἰθίοπάς θ’ ἱκόμην καὶ Σιδονίους καὶ Ἐρεμβοὺς
καὶ Λιβύην, ἵνα τ’ ἄρνες ἄφαρ κεραοὶ τελέθουσι.
sentences.l:
and to the Ethiopians I came, and the Sidonians, and the Erembians,
and to Libya, where the lambs at once come to be horned.
sentences.i: and I came to the Ethiopians, and the Sidonians, and the Erembians, and to Libya, where lambs grow their horns almost as soon as they are born.
sentences.n: ἱκόμην is the unaugmented aorist, 'I came'. Ἐρεμβοί is a people the ancients themselves could not agree on, some taking them for Arabs, others for a corruption of a different name; who they were is simply not known. κεραοὶ τελέθουσι, 'come to be horned', with ἄφαρ 'at once, straightway', is one of several marvels the Odyssey attaches to distant lands. Sidon, in Phoenicia, is named for its people, the Sidonians, distinct here from the Phoenicians of line 83.

sentences.t: τρὶς γὰρ τίκτει μῆλα τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτόν.
sentences.l: for three times within the full-completed year the flocks bring forth young.
sentences.i: for three times in a single full year the flocks give birth.
sentences.n: τίκτει is present, stating a general truth. μῆλα is 'sheep and goats' generally, as elsewhere in this part's flock language. τελεσφόρον...ἐνιαυτόν, 'the year that brings its round to completion', describes a full year's cycle; the claim of three lambings a year is part of the marvel of Libya's fertility, continuing the wonder of the horned newborn lambs.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν οὔτε ἄναξ ἐπιδευὴς οὔτε τι ποιμὴν
τυροῦ καὶ κρειῶν οὐδὲ γλυκεροῖο γάλακτος,
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ παρέχουσιν ἐπηετανὸν γάλα θῆσθαι.
sentences.l:
There neither master is in want, nor any shepherd,
of cheese and of meat, nor of sweet milk,
but always the flocks provide milk enough to be milked, unfailing.
sentences.i: There neither the master nor any herdsman is ever short of cheese or meat or sweet milk, for the flocks always give milk enough for the milking, and it never fails.
sentences.n: ἐπιδευής, 'in want, lacking', takes the genitives τυροῦ, κρειῶν, γάλακτος. ἄναξ is 'master, lord (of the flock)'; ποιμήν the ordinary word for 'shepherd, herdsman'. παρέχουσιν is an unaugmented present, 'they (the flocks) provide'; ἐπηετανόν, 'continuous, unfailing', modifies γάλα; θῆσθαι is a middle infinitive of purpose, 'for the sucking, milking of it'.

sentences.t:
ἧος ἐγὼ περὶ κεῖνα πολὺν βίοτον συναγείρων
ἠλώμην, τῆός μοι ἀδελφεὸν ἄλλος ἔπεφνεν
λάθρῃ, ἀνωιστί, δόλῳ οὐλομένης ἀλόχοιο·
sentences.i: But while I was wandering about those lands, gathering great wealth, all the while another man was killing my brother, secretly, without warning, by the treachery of his accursed wife;
sentences.n: ἧος...τῆος, 'while...meanwhile', is a correlative pair of temporal particles (Attic ἕως...τέως). συναγείρων is a present participle, 'gathering together'; βίοτον is 'livelihood, substance', the wealth Menelaus mentioned collecting on his travels. ἠλώμην is an unaugmented imperfect of ἀλάομαι, 'I was wandering'. ἔπεφνεν is a root aorist of θείνω/φένω, 'slew'; the brother is Agamemnon, unnamed here, and his 'accursed wife' is Clytemnestra, also unnamed; λάθρῃ and ἀνωιστί both stress the secrecy and surprise of Aegisthus's plot, already told in full at 1.29–43 of this poem.

sentences.t: ὣς οὔ τοι χαίρων τοῖσδε κτεάτεσσιν ἀνάσσω.
sentences.l: So not, be sure, with joy do I rule over these possessions.
sentences.i: So it is not with any joy that I am lord of these possessions.
sentences.n: ὥς here is the adverb 'so, thus' (Attic οὕτως), summing up what precedes. οὔ τοι, 'not, I assure you', negates χαίρων, 'rejoicing'; ἀνάσσω, 'I am lord, I rule', takes the dative κτεάτεσσιν, 'over these possessions'. The line turns Menelaus's earlier hint (line 81, 'perhaps not') into open admission: his wealth is real, his happiness in it is not.

sentences.t:
καὶ πατέρων τάδε μέλλετ’ ἀκουέμεν, οἵ τινες ὑμῖν
εἰσίν, ἐπεὶ μάλα πολλὰ πάθον, καὶ ἀπώλεσα οἶκον
εὖ μάλα ναιετάοντα, κεχανδότα πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλά.
sentences.l:
And from your fathers, whoever for you
they are, this you must be likely to have heard, since very much I suffered, and I lost a house
very well inhabited, holding much and good.
sentences.i: And you must surely have heard this from whatever fathers of yours are living, since I suffered a great deal, and lost a house that was very well settled, and held much fine wealth.
sentences.n: μέλλετ’ ἀκουέμεν, 'you are likely to have heard', with the infinitive in -έμεν, treats the tale as already known by hearsay; οἵ τινες ὑμῖν εἰσίν, 'whoever your fathers are', is delicately put, since Telemachus's own father's fate is exactly what is unknown. πάθον is the unaugmented aorist of πάσχω. ἀπώλεσα, an ordinary augmented aorist, 'I lost, destroyed'; εὖ μάλα ναιετάοντα, 'very well settled, inhabited', and κεχανδότα, the perfect participle of χανδάνω 'hold, contain', describe the house's former comfort and abundance.

sentences.t:
ὧν ὄφελον τριτάτην περ ἔχων ἐν δώμασι μοῖραν
ναίειν, οἱ δ’ ἄνδρες σόοι ἔμμεναι, οἳ τότ’ ὄλοντο
Τροίῃ ἐν εὐρείῃ ἑκὰς Ἄργεος ἱπποβότοιο.
sentences.l:
Of which I wish that a third part, at least, holding, in my halls,
I dwelt, and that the men were safe, who then perished
in Troy the broad, far from Argos the horse-pasturing.
sentences.i: I wish I lived with only a third part of it in my halls, and that the men were safe who then perished in broad Troy, far from horse-pasturing Argos.
sentences.n: ὄφελον with the infinitive ναίειν is the epic construction for an unattainable wish, 'would that I dwelt', regularly used without ἄν or κε. τριτάτην...μοῖραν, 'a third part, a third share', with περ giving it emphasis, 'even just a third'. σόοι ἔμμεναι is 'to be safe', the infinitive again in a wish construction, parallel to ναίειν. ἱπποβότοιο, 'horse-pasturing', is a standing epithet of Argos, from ἵππος and βόσκω.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔμπης πάντας μὲν ὀδυρόμενος καὶ ἀχεύων
πολλάκις ἐν μεγάροισι καθήμενος ἡμετέροισιν
ἄλλοτε μέν τε γόῳ φρένα τέρπομαι, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε
παύομαι·
sentences.l:
But nonetheless, all of them lamenting and grieving,
often in the halls sitting, in our own,
at one time, then, with wailing my heart I ease, at another
I cease;
sentences.i: But even so, grieving and mourning them all, sitting often in our own halls, sometimes I ease my heart with weeping, and sometimes I stop;
sentences.n: ἔμπης, 'nonetheless, all the same', concedes that the wish just made cannot be fulfilled. ὀδυρόμενος and ἀχεύων are present participles, 'lamenting' and 'grieving'; γόῳ φρένα τέρπομαι is a striking phrase, 'I delight my heart with wailing', where τέρπομαι, elsewhere a word for pleasure at feasts and song, is turned here to grief itself. ἄλλοτε μέν...ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε, 'at one time...at another', marks the alternation between weeping and its relief.

sentences.t: αἰψηρὸς δὲ κόρος κρυεροῖο γόοιο.
sentences.l: for quick is the surfeit of chilling lament.
sentences.i: for one's fill of cold weeping comes quickly.
sentences.n: αἰψηρός, 'swift, quick', modifies κόρος, 'satiety, surfeit'; κρυεροῖο, 'chilling, causing a shudder', describes γόος, 'lament, wailing'. The line is a small, detached observation on grief's limits: a person tires of weeping before the grief itself is spent.

sentences.t:
τῶν πάντων οὐ τόσσον ὀδύρομαι, ἀχνύμενός περ,
ὡς ἑνός, ὅς τέ μοι ὕπνον ἀπεχθαίρει καὶ ἐδωδὴν
μνωομένῳ, ἐπεὶ οὔ τις Ἀχαιῶν τόσσ’ ἐμόγησεν,
ὅσσ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἐμόγησε καὶ ἤρατο.
sentences.l:
For all of them I do not grieve so much, grieved though I am,
as for one, who makes sleep hateful to me, and food,
whenever I remember him, since no one of the Achaeans toiled so much
as Odysseus toiled and endured.
sentences.i: Of all of them I do not grieve so much, grieved as I am, as for one man, who, whenever I think of him, makes sleep and food hateful to me, since no Achaean toiled as Odysseus toiled and endured.
sentences.n: τόσσον...ὡς is a comparative construction, 'not so much...as'; ἀχνύμενός περ is concessive, 'grieved though I am (for all of them)'. ἀπεχθαίρει, 'makes hateful', governs both ὕπνον and ἐδωδήν. μνωομένῳ is a present participle agreeing with the implied 'to me', 'as I call him to mind'. ἐμόγησεν and ἐμόγησε are both aorists of μογέω 'toil, labor'. This is the first time in the part that Odysseus is named outright by Menelaus, at the emotional center of his speech.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλεν
αὐτῷ κήδε’ ἔσεσθαι, ἐμοὶ δ’ ἄχος αἰὲν ἄλαστον
κείνου, ὅπως δὴ δηρὸν ἀποίχεται, οὐδέ τι ἴδμεν,
ζώει ὅ γ’ ἦ τέθνηκεν.
sentences.l:
And for him, then, as it seems, it was fated
sorrows to be, but for me, grief forever unforgettable,
for that man, in that he has now for long been gone, nor do we know at all
whether he lives or has died.
sentences.i: And it seems he himself was fated to have sorrows of his own, but for me it means a grief forever unforgettable, for him — that he has now been gone so long, and we do not know at all whether he lives or is dead.
sentences.n: ἔμελλεν, an unaugmented imperfect, 'was destined, fated'; the dative αὐτῷ is 'for himself', Odysseus. κήδεα is 'sorrows, troubles'; ἐμοὶ δέ contrasts Menelaus's own grief with Odysseus's own sufferings. ἄλαστον, 'unforgettable', is from ἀ- and λανθάνομαι. ὅπως δή, 'in that, seeing that', gives the reason for the grief. ἴδμεν is the epic form of ἴσμεν, 'we know'; the alternative ζώει...ἦ τέθνηκεν, 'whether he lives or has died', states outright the uncertainty that drives the whole poem's plot.

sentences.t:
ὀδύρονταί νύ που αὐτὸν
Λαέρτης θ’ ὁ γέρων καὶ ἐχέφρων Πηνελόπεια
Τηλέμαχός θ’, ὃν ἔλειπε νέον γεγαῶτ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
sentences.l:
For him, surely, somewhere now they are lamenting,
both Laertes, the old man, and sound-minded Penelope,
and Telemachus, whom he left newly-born in his house.
sentences.i: No doubt they are grieving for him even now — Laertes the old man, and sound-minded Penelope, and Telemachus, whom he left a newborn child in his house.
sentences.n: ὀδύρονται is an unaugmented present, 'they are lamenting'; νύ που, 'surely, I suppose', softens the claim with the same uncertainty as the line before. ἐχέφρων, 'sound of mind, sensible' (ἔχω + φρήν), is a new epithet for Penelope in this poem, kept distinct from the already-fixed περίφρων Πηνελόπεια, 'circumspect Penelope', since Homer uses two different compounds of φρήν for her. γεγαῶτ’ is a perfect participle of γίγνομαι, 'having been born'; νέον is adverbial, 'newly'. The part ends here still inside Menelaus's speech, which continues well beyond line 112 in the poem; no closing quotation mark is given, since — unlike every other speech in this part — this one does not close within 4.1–112.
